claims.text: The corrosion resistance of high-chromium steels is primarily governed by formation and rapid regeneration of a chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
The passive layer on high-chromium steels consists mainly of Cr2O3.
The relevant initial state has sufficient chromium, a naturally formed continuous passive film, and a homogeneous microstructure.
Mechanical polishing and/or chemical cleaning can be used to remove the native oxide and disrupt passivation.
Oxygen availability under the proposed exposure conditions permits passive-film regeneration.
Chromium rapidly oxidizes at active sites such as grain boundaries during corrosive exposure.
Chromium oxidation produces a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 film.
The Cr2O3 film acts as a barrier to ion and electron transport.
An intact chromium-oxide passivation film minimizes further corrosion.
Rapid regeneration of the chromium-oxide film minimizes further corrosion after surface damage.
Removing the passive film disrupts corrosion protection.
Samples retaining or rapidly regenerating Cr2O3 will have lower weight loss and lower corrosion current density than samples whose film is removed and prevented from reforming.
The mechanism should hold only when chromium content is adequate and the environment does not aggressively disrupt the passive film.
Moderate chloride concentrations and temperatures conducive to diffusion-driven passivation fall within the proposed validity range.
In extreme environments, dissolution, redox effects, or other degradation mechanisms may dominate over passive-film protection.
The effects of grain size and minor alloying elements on passive-film reformation kinetics remain incompletely quantified.
XPS or SEM can be used to monitor passive-film composition and formation during the controlled comparison.
Weight loss, electrochemical response, surface composition, and film thickness are proposed as measurable outcomes.
No significant corrosion-rate difference between intact-film and film-removed groups is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The prediction invokes a comparison against samples in which passive-film reformation is hindered, but the experimental design only removes the initial film and then uses oxygenated conditions that explicitly permit regeneration; it does not include an intervention that hinders reformation.

The hypothesis predicts that rapid regeneration restores protection, so rapid reformation could eliminate the difference between initially intact and initially cleaned samples. The falsification rule nevertheless treats an absence of a corrosion-rate difference as falsifying without distinguishing this predicted regeneration scenario.
